lines.text: At about a quarter past seven on the morning of the thirtieth of June, nineteen-oh-eight, something came out of a clear sky over central Siberia and exploded above the forest. It flattened more than two thousand square kilometres of taiga.
Investigators came. They found no crater. No meteorite was ever pulled out of the ground. And into that silence moved a famous idea: that this was not a rock at all, but a crashed spacecraft.
A nuclear engine failing over Siberia. Alien wreckage hidden in the swamps. Even a ship that sacrificed itself to save the Earth. You have heard the versions.
So tonight we treat Tunguska the way investigators treat a crash. We open a file. We take witness statements, survey the site, search for wreckage, rebuild the flight path, and read the recorders.
Then we line up the suspects: comet, asteroid, or craft. And at the end, like any accident board, we state a probable cause.

Section one: the occurrence. The place is the basin of the Podkamennaya Tunguska river, a tributary of the Yenisei, in the Russian Empire. Swamp, permafrost and low wooded hills, frozen eight or nine months a year.

The people here were mostly Evenki reindeer herders, living in small family groups in conical tents, and a few Russian traders at posts like Vanavara, about sixty kilometres south of what would become ground zero.
That morning, under a clear sky, a fireball brighter than the Sun crossed from the south-east, trailing white. People saw it from hundreds of kilometres away.
At about seven fourteen local time, it exploded. A column of fire, a cloud rising tens of kilometres, a heat pulse felt eighty kilometres away. Windows broke as far as two hundred kilometres out.
At least three people died, all Evenki, and reindeer herds were lost. It was the most violent impact event in recorded history. And almost nobody outside Siberia knew exactly where it had happened.
Then the file sat closed for thirteen years. War, revolution and civil war came first. The first scientific expedition would not set out until nineteen twenty-one.

Section two: witness statements. More than seven hundred accounts were collected between nineteen-oh-eight and the nineteen-seventies. The most famous comes from Semyon Semyonov, a farmer at the Vanavara trading post.

He was sitting on the porch at breakfast, about to hoop a barrel, when, in his words, the sky was split in two, and the whole northern part of the sky seemed covered with fire. He felt heat, as if his shirt had caught fire.
Then a bang, a mighty crash, and he was thrown about six metres from the porch and lost consciousness. Window panes at the trading post blew out. The iron hasp on the barn door broke.

Closer in, an Evenki man called Chuchan was asleep in his tent. He described being thrown into the hearth, trees falling, needles and reindeer moss burning, and heat, as he put it, enough to burn alive.
Notice what these statements describe: an object moving across the sky, then a blast in the air. Not a light that hovered. Not a craft that turned. A fireball on a straight line.

Some witnesses thought another planet had struck the Earth. Many Evenki saw the anger of Ogdy, their god of fire and thunder. Every age reads a sky like that through its own beliefs. Ours reads it through science fiction.
Memory fades, and the later accounts are less reliable. But the core never changes: a fireball, a wave of heat, and a blast from the north.
Section three: the site survey. In nineteen twenty-seven, the mineralogist Leonid Kulik finally reached the blast zone with Evenki guides. He expected a giant crater, and a fortune in meteoric iron.

There was no crater. At the centre, trees were still standing, upright, but stripped of every branch, like telegraph poles. Farther out, the forest lay flat, every trunk pointing away from the centre.
Later surveys mapped the fallen zone at about two thousand one hundred and fifty square kilometres, shaped like a butterfly with a wingspan of seventy kilometres.
Kulik believed some boggy holes were meteorite craters. He drained one, called Suslov's crater, thirty-two metres wide. At the bottom he found an old tree stump. Not a crater after all.

In nineteen thirty-eight he arranged an aerial survey: fifteen hundred photographic negatives of the central zone. The original negatives were burned in nineteen seventy-five, as flammable nitrate film. Prints survive in Tomsk.
Kulik never closed the file. In the Second World War he joined the militia, was captured, and died of typhus in a prisoner-of-war camp in nineteen forty-two.

Here is the key forensic clue. Standing trees in the middle, flattened trees in a ring: that is what a blast from above does. In the nineteen-sixties, Soviet scientists rebuilt it with model forests of matches and small charges, and got the same butterfly.
The blast came from the air, several kilometres up, angled in from the south-east. So whatever it was never touched the ground in one piece.
Section four: the wreckage. A crash investigator's first question is simple. Where are the pieces? Expeditions in the nineteen-fifties and sixties sifted the soil.
They found microscopic silicate and magnetite spheres, rich in nickel compared with iron, the kind of ratio found in meteorites. And their spread in the soil matched debris from an air burst.

In the nineteen-nineties, Italian researchers led by Giuseppe Longo of the University of Bologna extracted resin from trees that lived through the blast. Trapped inside: material typical of rocky asteroids, and rare in comets.
Peat bogs hold a nineteen-oh-eight layer with odd carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen isotopes, and reported iridium. To be fair, other laboratories have not confirmed all of those results.
And the boulder known as John's stone, once hoped to be a piece of the impactor, turned out to be ordinary Earth rock, a quartzite.

Then there is Lake Cheko, about eight kilometres from the epicentre. In two thousand and seven, a Bologna team proposed it was a crater dug by a ten-metre fragment, citing its funnel-shaped bottom and its sediment.
In twenty seventeen, Russian scientists counted at least two hundred and eighty yearly layers in the lake bed, which would make it older than the blast. The argument continues.
So there is no big wreck. Just dust. To a crash investigator, that is a clue in itself: something blew apart so completely that nothing large was left.
And notice what is not on this wreckage list. No alloy. No hull plate. No engine part. Not from more than a century of searching.
Section five: the flight path. Cross-checking witnesses, the tree-fall and computer models gives a direction. The body came in from the south-east, at a shallow angle of roughly thirty degrees.

It exploded somewhere between five and ten kilometres up. Models suggest a body around fifty to sixty metres across, moving at more than eleven kilometres a second. Energy estimates run from about three to thirty megatons, most often ten to fifteen.
Now, comet or asteroid? In nineteen thirty-four, F. J. W. Whipple proposed a small comet: ice and dust that would vaporise and leave little behind. It might explain the glowing night skies too.
In nineteen seventy-eight, Lubor Kresák linked it to Comet Encke, parent of the Beta Taurid meteor shower, which peaks at the very end of June.

But in nineteen eighty-three, Zdeněk Sekanina argued that a fragile comet on such a shallow path should have broken up higher. A dense, stony asteroid fits better. A two thousand and one orbit study put the odds at eighty-three percent asteroid, seventeen percent comet.

And in nineteen ninety-three, Christopher Chyba and colleagues showed how a stony asteroid can blow itself apart in mid-air. Once the air pressure outstrips its strength, it releases almost all its energy at once. No crater. Wide damage. Exactly what Kulik found.
There is even a twenty twenty model of an iron asteroid that grazed the atmosphere and flew back out into space. One flight path, several explanations. All of them natural.

Section six: the recorders. Air crashes have black boxes. Tunguska had instruments thousands of kilometres away. Seismographs at Irkutsk, Tashkent, Tiflis and Jena recorded a shock close to magnitude five.
Barographs in Britain and Germany, and as far away as Washington and Batavia, logged the air-pressure wave as it rolled around the globe.
And for several nights, skies over western Eurasia glowed so brightly that people could read a newspaper at midnight. In England, astronomers gave up observing because the sky was too bright.
Measurements at Mount Wilson in California later suggested a drop in the clarity of the air, consistent with fine dust spread through the upper atmosphere.
One recorder matters most for the alien file. A nuclear explosion leaves radioactivity. So, in nineteen fifty-nine, young volunteers from Tomsk, led by Gennady Plekhanov, walked in with radiometers.

Their first readings looked raised. But they found no engine nozzles, and no radioactivity clearly tied to nineteen-oh-eight. Radioactivity in the trees was traced to fallout from the bomb tests of the nineteen-fifties.
Section seven: the suspects. Start with the craft. The spaceship idea has a birthday: January nineteen forty-six, a short story called Explosion, by the Soviet writer Alexander Kazantsev.
Kazantsev had read about Hiroshima. He imagined a nuclear-powered ship from Mars blowing up over the taiga. It was fiction. But it was so vivid that many readers took it as a hypothesis.
To be fair to him, Kazantsev saw something real: an explosion in the air explains the missing crater. But a natural air burst explains it too, without radiation. And the radiation was never there.

In two thousand and four, Yuri Lavbin of a Siberian foundation called Tunguska Space Phenomenon announced blocks of an extraterrestrial device near the village of Poligus. He had said in advance that he intended to prove a spaceship crashed.
The space writer James Oberg pointed out that the region lies under drop zones for spent rocket stages launched from Baikonur. We could find no peer-reviewed analysis of the find.

Other suspects. Nikola Tesla's death ray, fired from Wardenclyffe Tower? That story was invented in a fictionalised biography in the nineteen-nineties. Tesla never finished the tower, and wrote of no such beam in nineteen-oh-eight.

Physicists tried exotic ideas too. In nineteen sixty-five, a chunk of antimatter. In nineteen seventy-three, a tiny black hole passing through the Earth. Neither left the signature it predicts: no confirmed radiocarbon spike, no exit blast in the North Atlantic.
And a few geophysicists proposed natural gas erupting from the ground. But nearly every witness saw something cross the sky first.

Then, in February twenty thirteen, nature ran a test. An asteroid about eighteen metres wide exploded some thirty kilometres above Chelyabinsk, in Russia. About four to five hundred kilotons. Around fifteen hundred people hurt, mostly by flying glass. And meteorites were recovered.
Section eight: probable cause. The file is complete. Let's score the findings.

A fireball crossing the sky, seen by hundreds: evidence. Standing trees ringed by a flattened butterfly: evidence of an air burst. Nickel-rich spheres and asteroid-type particles in resin: evidence of a cosmic body. A stony asteroid some fifty to sixty metres wide: the most likely culprit.
A nuclear alien spaceship: no evidence, and no radioactivity. The two thousand and four alien device: unverified, never published. Asteroid versus comet, and Lake Cheko: still open.

Probable cause: a natural object from space, most likely a stony asteroid, exploded five to ten kilometres above the taiga with the force of a large nuclear weapon. There was no crash, because nothing big enough to crash ever reached the ground.
The craft entered this file in nineteen forty-six, as a story. Every test that could have found it, radioactivity, wreckage, metal, came back empty.

Every accident report ends with recommendations. This one already has them. Since twenty sixteen, the thirtieth of June has been the United Nations' International Asteroid Day, a reminder to keep watching the sky.

Blasts the size of Tunguska are thought to happen roughly once every few centuries, perhaps once in a thousand years. This one fell on an almost empty forest. The real mystery of Tunguska is not who was flying. It is whether, next time, we will see it coming.
Comet, asteroid, or craft? Give us your verdict in the comments, and subscribe for the next case file.
